questions.prompt: Continuous training (CT) in MLOps means:

options.text: Retraining on a fixed schedule only
Automatically retraining when drift or performance thresholds trigger it

questions.explanation: CT watches production metrics and retrains when quality degrades — closing the loop between inference and training.

questions.prompt: A feature store solves which main problem?

options.text: Online/offline feature consistency and reuse across teams

questions.explanation: Feature stores ensure the same feature logic is used in training and serving, avoiding training-serving skew.

questions.prompt: Model registries typically store:

options.text: Model artifacts + metadata (metrics, stage, lineage, signatures)

questions.explanation: Metadata matters as much as artifacts — you need to know how a model was trained, its metrics, and how to reproduce it.

questions.prompt: Data versioning (e.g., DVC) matters because:

options.text: Models are not reproducible without the exact training data

questions.explanation: Reproducibility requires versioning data as rigorously as code — otherwise you cannot rerun training and expect identical results.

questions.prompt: Shadow deployment means:

options.text: Run the new model alongside the current one without affecting live traffic

questions.explanation: Shadow mode logs the new model's predictions without serving them, letting you compare against production safely.

questions.prompt: Canary deployment releases a new model to:

options.text: A small percentage of traffic, then expands if metrics stay healthy

questions.explanation: Canary rollouts limit blast radius. If key metrics regress, you roll back before most users are affected.

questions.prompt: The difference between A/B testing and canary is:

options.text: A/B tests compare business outcomes between variants; canary focuses on health metrics for rollout safety

questions.explanation: A/B is about comparing; canary is about safety. Both use traffic splitting but with different success criteria.

questions.prompt: Model cards are:

options.text: Short documents describing a model's intended use, limitations, and evaluation

questions.explanation: Model cards improve transparency and responsible ML — used by Google, Hugging Face, and others.

questions.prompt: Training-serving skew refers to:

options.text: Differences in feature computation between training and production

questions.explanation: Even tiny differences (e.g., different tokenizers or missing values) can cause production behavior to diverge from validation.

questions.prompt: Automated retraining pipelines should always include:

options.text: Validation gates, regression tests, and rollback safety

questions.explanation: Automation without validation ships broken models. Gates ensure the new model actually improves on the old one.

questions.prompt: Data drift is best detected by monitoring:

options.text: The distribution of input features vs a training reference

questions.explanation: Statistical tests (KS, PSI) compare live feature distributions against the training distribution.

questions.prompt: Concept drift occurs when:

options.text: The relationship between features and target changes

questions.explanation: Same inputs no longer map to the same outputs — e.g., user preferences change, or economic conditions shift.

questions.prompt: p99 latency in an ML API is:

options.text: The latency below which 99% of requests complete

questions.explanation: p99 captures tail behavior, which users notice more than average latency.

questions.prompt: A key reason to log predictions in production is:

options.text: To enable debugging, drift monitoring, and offline retraining

questions.explanation: Without logs, you can't diagnose failures, measure drift, or build high-quality retraining sets.

questions.prompt: The feedback loop problem in ML systems refers to:

options.text: Predictions influencing future data in ways that bias training

questions.explanation: Example: a recommender promotes certain items, users click them, and future training data over-represents those items — reinforcing the original bias.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a typical ML service SLO?
questions.explanation: SLOs measure user-facing reliability: latency, availability, error rate, throughput.

questions.prompt: Why do you need a fallback path in production ML?

options.text: So the service degrades gracefully when the model or its dependencies fail

questions.explanation: Fallbacks could be a cached prediction, a simpler model, or a heuristic — never returning a hard error to the user.

questions.prompt: Feature flags let you:

options.text: Toggle behavior at runtime without redeploying

questions.explanation: Feature flags enable gradual rollouts, A/B tests, and quick kill-switches for bad model versions.

questions.prompt: The purpose of a staging environment for ML is:

options.text: Mirror production to catch issues before they reach users

questions.explanation: Staging should match production in data pipelines, traffic patterns, and infrastructure so issues surface before deploy.

questions.prompt: Model monitoring should include which signals?

options.text: Data drift, concept drift, prediction distribution, latency, and business KPIs

questions.explanation: Comprehensive monitoring catches problems at multiple layers, not just the model's raw output.

questions.prompt: REST vs gRPC for ML serving:

options.text: gRPC is generally faster and uses schema (protobuf), but REST is simpler and more universal

questions.explanation: gRPC's binary protocol and streaming are popular for high-throughput ML services; REST is universal and easier to debug.

questions.prompt: Batching inference requests:

options.text: Improves GPU utilization and throughput at the cost of slightly higher per-request latency

questions.explanation: Batching fills hardware better — great for offline or throughput-bound systems, less ideal for latency-sensitive ones.

questions.prompt: Serverless deployment of ML models:

options.text: Reduces ops overhead but has cold-start latency and often worse for large models

questions.explanation: Serverless (Lambda, Cloud Functions) is convenient but has limits on memory, startup time, and concurrent execution.

questions.prompt: Model quantization (e.g., FP32 → INT8) during deployment:

options.text: Reduces model size and inference cost, sometimes with small accuracy loss

questions.explanation: Quantization trades some numerical precision for dramatic speed and memory gains — often a key production optimization.

questions.prompt: A containerized model + an HTTP layer is the most common deployment pattern because:

options.text: Containers are portable, reproducible, and easy to scale behind a load balancer

questions.explanation: Docker + FastAPI/Flask + Kubernetes or ECS is the industry standard pattern for ML microservices.

questions.prompt: Streaming inference vs batch inference:

options.text: Streaming processes data continuously as it arrives; batch processes in chunks on a schedule

questions.explanation: Streaming fits real-time (Kafka, Kinesis); batch fits nightly or hourly jobs.

questions.prompt: The main purpose of an inference API gateway is:

options.text: Handle auth, rate limiting, routing, and observability in front of the model

questions.explanation: Gateways isolate model code from cross-cutting concerns, so the model service stays simple.

questions.prompt: Predictive caching (memoizing model outputs) is best suited for:
questions.explanation: Cache hit rates matter — repeated queries can skip the model call entirely, cutting latency and cost.

questions.prompt: Autoscaling an ML service should consider:

options.text: Request queue depth, latency, and GPU/CPU utilization

questions.explanation: Pure CPU-based scaling misses GPU-bound or queue-bound workloads. Use queue + latency-based metrics.

questions.prompt: A readiness probe in Kubernetes tells the cluster:

options.text: That the service is ready to receive traffic
That the pod is being deleted

questions.explanation: Without readiness, traffic can hit a pod before the model finishes loading, causing 500s.

questions.prompt: Recall is defined as:
questions.explanation: Recall (sensitivity) measures what fraction of actual positives were caught.

questions.prompt: F1 score is:

options.text: Arithmetic mean of precision and recall
Harmonic mean of precision and recall

questions.explanation: Harmonic mean penalizes imbalance — F1 is low if either precision or recall is low.

questions.prompt: MAE vs RMSE:

options.text: RMSE penalizes large errors more due to squaring

questions.explanation: RMSE squares errors, so outliers have disproportionate impact; MAE treats all errors linearly.

questions.prompt: AUC-ROC of 0.5 means:
questions.explanation: AUC = 0.5 means the model cannot distinguish classes better than chance. AUC < 0.5 means it's systematically wrong.

questions.prompt: The main reason accuracy is misleading for imbalanced data:

options.text: A trivially 'always predict majority' model can score high

questions.explanation: If 99% of samples are negative, predicting 'always negative' gives 99% accuracy while catching zero positives.

questions.prompt: The ROC curve plots:

options.text: True positive rate vs false positive rate across thresholds

questions.explanation: Each point corresponds to a decision threshold. AUC summarizes the whole curve in one number.

questions.prompt: PR curve is preferred over ROC when:
questions.explanation: ROC can look optimistic under class imbalance. PR focuses on the rare positive class, giving a clearer picture.

questions.prompt: A confusion matrix for binary classification has:
questions.explanation: True/False × Positive/Negative = 4 cells. All key classification metrics derive from these.

questions.prompt: Calibration of a classifier's probabilities means:

options.text: Ensuring predicted probabilities match observed frequencies

questions.explanation: A well-calibrated model that says '70%' should be right ~70% of the time. Reliability diagrams and Brier score check this.

questions.prompt: For a regression model, R² can be negative. What does it mean?

options.text: The model performs worse than predicting the mean

questions.explanation: R² < 0 means the model's predictions are worse than just using the target's mean — a sign something is wrong.

questions.prompt: Pruning a neural network means:

options.text: Removing low-magnitude weights or unimportant neurons

questions.explanation: Pruning creates sparsity — often 50–90% of weights can be removed with minimal accuracy loss.

questions.prompt: Knowledge distillation trains:

options.text: A small 'student' model to mimic a larger 'teacher' model

questions.explanation: Students learn from the teacher's soft probability distributions, often outperforming training directly on hard labels.

questions.prompt: Post-training quantization (PTQ) vs quantization-aware training (QAT):

options.text: PTQ quantizes after training; QAT simulates quantization during training for better accuracy

questions.explanation: QAT usually preserves accuracy better but requires retraining; PTQ is faster to apply.

questions.prompt: Which of these reduces inference latency WITHOUT changing the model's numerical precision?
questions.explanation: Fusing ops removes memory round-trips without losing precision — a common graph optimization.

questions.prompt: ONNX is used to:

options.text: Represent models in an interoperable format across frameworks

questions.explanation: ONNX lets you export from PyTorch/TF and run with optimized runtimes like ONNX Runtime or TensorRT.

questions.prompt: TensorRT is:

options.text: NVIDIA's inference optimizer for GPU deployment

questions.explanation: TensorRT fuses ops, uses mixed precision, and tunes kernels for NVIDIA GPUs — often 2–5× speedup over raw PyTorch inference.

questions.prompt: Structured vs unstructured pruning:

options.text: Structured removes whole neurons/channels; unstructured removes individual weights (sparse matrices)

questions.explanation: Structured pruning yields dense smaller models that run fast on any hardware. Unstructured needs sparse-aware kernels.

questions.prompt: A mixed-precision forward pass (FP16 + FP32):

options.text: Uses lower precision where safe, keeping sensitive ops in FP32

questions.explanation: Automatic mixed precision on modern GPUs doubles throughput with negligible accuracy loss.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a model compression technique?
questions.explanation: Data augmentation improves training; the other three shrink the deployed model.

questions.prompt: Latency-critical ML services often prefer smaller models because:

options.text: Inference cost scales with model size and memory bandwidth

questions.explanation: For user-facing products, shaving 50ms of latency often beats a 0.5% accuracy improvement.
